lessons.title: Lesson 1: Starting from a problem, not from AI
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Pick a real customer problem that an AI-assisted service could solve.
This lesson builds toward: Given five customer problems you could solve, you will choose one real, frequent and painful problem for an AI-assisted service, after asking at least one real person how they handle it today.
The most common mistake is starting with "I want to sell something with AI". Start instead with a problem people already pay to fix, or complain about often: "Small restaurants don't have time to post on social media." "Job seekers don't know how to describe their skills."
Good problems are frequent, painful and specific. Ask: Who has this problem? How do they solve it now? What does that cost them in money or time? Would they pay me to solve it faster or better?
AI can help you brainstorm and sort ideas, but talk to at least three real people who have the problem before you build anything.
Step by step:
- List five problems you have seen people or businesses struggle with.
- Ask AI to help rate each: how often, how painful, how they solve it now.
- Pick the top one.
- Talk to three people who have it and ask how they deal with it today.
Words to know:
- Problem worth solving: a frequent, painful, specific problem people already spend money or time on.
Try it now: List five problems, use AI to help rate them, pick one, and ask at least one real person who has that problem how they handle it today.
You can now choose a real customer problem to build an AI-assisted service around.

check.q: What makes a customer problem worth building a service around?
options: It is frequent, painful and specific
It is something AI is famous for
check.why: Frequent, painful, specific problems are ones people pay to fix.

check.q: You have a great idea but have not talked to anyone with the problem. What do you do next?
options: Ask real people how they handle it today
check.why: Talking to real people first tells you if the problem is real.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Designing where AI helps and where you check
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Map your service as steps, marking which are AI and which are human.
This lesson builds toward: Given your chosen problem, you will map the service as numbered steps marked AI, human or tool, with inputs and a deliverable, with a human check before anything is delivered.
An AI-assisted service is a set of steps. Example, a social media package for a restaurant: 1) get photos and the week's specials from the owner (human), 2) draft captions (AI), 3) check facts, prices and tone (human), 4) make graphics in Canva (AI-helped), 5) send for approval (human), 6) schedule posts (tool).
Put a person at every step where a mistake could hurt the customer: facts, prices, health, legal or money matters, and anything published under the customer's name. This "human in the loop" is what customers are paying for: speed from AI, judgment from you.
Write down what goes in at the start (what you need from the customer) and what comes out at the end (exactly what they get).
Step by step:
- Write what you need from the customer at the start.
- List every step to deliver the service.
- Mark each step: AI, human, or tool.
- Add a human check before anything goes to the customer.
- Write exactly what the customer gets at the end.
Words to know:
- Human in the loop: a person checks or approves the AI's work before it is used.
- Deliverable: the finished thing the customer receives.
Try it now: Map your service as numbered steps. Mark each as AI, human or tool, and add a human check before delivery. Write the inputs and the deliverable.
You can now design an AI-assisted service with clear human checks.

options: The finished thing the customer receives
check.why: The deliverable is what the customer gets at the end.

check.q: Your service map sends AI-written menu prices straight to the client. What do you add?
options: A second AI to check the first
check.why: A person checks facts and prices before anything goes out.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Writing a reusable instruction prompt
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Write one instruction prompt you can reuse for every customer.
This lesson builds toward: Using a free AI assistant, you will write a reusable instruction prompt with role, rules, output format and slots, giving consistent results for two pretend customers.
To deliver the same quality every time, write one detailed instruction prompt and reuse it. It should include: the role ("You are helping me write social posts for small restaurants"), the rules (tone, length, what never to do), the format of the output, and a slot for each customer's details.
Example rules: "Never invent prices or menu items. Only use the specials I give you. Mark anything you are unsure about with [CHECK]." Rules like these make the AI's mistakes easier to catch.
Many assistants let you save custom instructions or build a saved assistant with your instructions; look in the tool's settings or help pages. If yours does not, keep the prompt in a document and paste it in each time.
Step by step:
- Write the role.
- Write the rules, including what the AI must never do.
- Describe the output format.
- Add [slots] for each customer's details.
- Test it on two pretend customers and tighten the rules.
Words to know:
- Instruction prompt: a detailed, reusable prompt that sets the AI's role, rules and output format.
- Slot: a marked place in the prompt where you paste each customer's details.
Try it now: Write your instruction prompt with role, rules, format and slots. Run it with details for two pretend customers and improve the rules where the output went wrong.
You can now write a reusable instruction prompt that gives consistent results for each customer.

check.q: What is a slot in an instruction prompt?
options: A blank you fill with each customer's details
check.why: Slots let you reuse one prompt for every customer.

check.q: Your prompt keeps inventing business hours. What do you change?
options: Nothing; fix it each time by hand
Add a rule: never invent hours; mark unknowns with [CHECK]
check.why: Clear rules stop repeated AI mistakes.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Testing with three real people
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Run your service for three people and learn what to fix.
This lesson builds toward: With up to three real people, you will run your service, time each step and record their feedback in their own words, writing at least one change and testing again.
Before you sell widely, run the whole service for three real people, for free or at a test price. Watch for: where the AI got things wrong, where you spent the most time, and what the customer liked or did not understand.
Ask each tester three questions: "What was most useful?" "What was confusing or wrong?" "Would you pay for this, and how much?" Write down their exact words.
Time each step. If the human checks take longer than doing it by hand, change the instruction prompt or the steps. Fix the top problems, then test again.
Step by step:
- Find three people with the problem.
- Run the full service for each one.
- Time each step and note every AI mistake.
- Ask the three questions and write down their answers.
- Fix the biggest problems and update your prompt.
Words to know:
- Tester: a real person who tries your product early and gives honest feedback.
- Feedback: what people tell you about what worked and what did not.
Try it now: Run your service for at least one real person (three if you can). Time each step, note the AI's mistakes, ask the three questions and write one change you will make.
You can now test an AI-assisted service with real people and improve it from their feedback.

check.q: What should you write down when testers give feedback?
check.why: Exact words show what customers really value and worry about.

check.q: Two testers say the result took too long. What do you do?
options: Find the slow step, change it and test again
check.why: Testing is for finding and fixing problems, then testing again.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Pricing your AI-assisted service
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Set a price that covers your costs and time and fits what customers will pay.
This lesson builds toward: Given your costs and testers' feedback, you will calculate a package price in a spreadsheet, covering all costs, including checking time, and leaving a profit.
Add up your costs per customer: your time (including checking the AI's work), tool subscriptions shared across customers, and any other costs. Then compare with what customers pay now for other ways of solving the problem, and what testers said they would pay.
Do not price only by how fast AI makes it. Customers pay for the result and your judgment, not for your minutes. A package ("12 posts a month") is often easier to sell than an hourly rate.
Have AI help with the math and with ideas for packages, but check every number yourself in a spreadsheet. For tax and business registration, check official sources such as irs.gov and your state's business office, or an accountant.
Step by step:
- List your costs per customer, including checking time.
- Find what customers pay now for other solutions.
- Note what testers said they would pay.
- Choose a package and a price, and check the math yourself.
- Make sure the price covers your costs with something left over.
Words to know:
- Package: a set bundle of work for a set price, like 12 posts a month.
- Profit: what is left after you pay all your costs.
Official sources:
- IRS: Self-Employed Individuals Tax Center
Try it now: Work out your cost per customer in a spreadsheet, compare with what testers said, and set a package price that leaves a profit.
You can now set a price for an AI-assisted service that covers your costs and fits the market.

options: What is left after paying all costs
The cost of the AI tool
check.why: Profit is the money left after every cost is covered.

check.q: Your price covers the AI tool but not the hour you spend checking. What do you do?
options: Add your checking time to the cost and reset the price
check.why: Checking time is a real cost that the price must cover.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Describing it honestly
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write a product description that tells the truth about what AI does.
This lesson builds toward: For your finished service, you will write a product description that says honestly what AI does and what a person checks, with no claims you cannot prove.
Customers trust you more when you are clear about how the service works: "We use AI to draft, and a person checks every post before it goes out." Do not pretend AI does more than it does, or that a person does the work when AI does.
The FTC enforces truth-in-advertising rules against misleading AI claims. In 2026 it finalized orders against companies that claimed an AI marketing service listened to people's conversations through smart devices when it did not. Claims about what your AI does, how accurate it is, or results customers will get must be true and backed by evidence.
Avoid "guaranteed", "100% accurate" and "replaces a lawyer/doctor/accountant". Talk to a lawyer if you are unsure whether a claim is allowed.
Step by step:
- Write what the customer gets in plain words.
- Say honestly where AI is used and where a person checks.
- Remove any claim you cannot prove with evidence.
- Have AI review it: "Point out any claim that could be misleading."
- Ask a lawyer if you are unsure.
Words to know:
- Misleading claim: a statement that gives people a false idea, even if each word is technically true.
- Evidence: tests, results or records that prove a claim.
Official sources:
- FTC: Advertising and Marketing Basics
- FTC: Orders against Cox Media Group and two other firms over AI marketing claims (2026)
Try it now: Final task: write your honest product description, then put together your one-page product sheet: problem, deliverable, steps (AI vs human), instruction prompt, test results, price and description.
You can now design, test, price and honestly describe an AI-assisted product or service.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Customer problem The problem is vague or not checked with a real person. One specific problem and what the customer gets, checked with real people. Includes how they solve it now and what that costs them. Steps and human checks Steps are not marked, or nothing is checked before delivery. Numbered steps marked AI, human or tool, with a human check before delivery. Says exactly what the human checks at each check point. Instruction prompt Missing rules or slots, or results vary a lot. Role, rules, format and slots, giving consistent results. Uses [CHECK] marks and has rules added from test mistakes. Test results No real person tested it, or no change was made. Results from tests with real people, their own words and at least one change. Three people tested it and a second test showed the change worked. Price and description Price ignores checking time, or the description overpromises. A package price covering all costs with profit, and an honest description. Shows the spreadsheet math and says clearly what AI does and what a person does. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

options: "Fully automatic, no human needed" when a person checks everything
"AI drafts, and a person checks every item before delivery"
check.why: It tells the truth about what AI and people each do.

check.q: You are unsure whether a claim on your sales page is allowed. What do you do?
options: Keep it and see what happens
Remove it or check with a lawyer
check.why: When in doubt, leave it out or get legal advice.
